title: Anaxagoras
orientation: This chapter covers Anaxagoras, the Ionian philosopher who, per Russell, was 'the first to introduce philosophy to the Athenians' and the first to propose mind (nous) as the cause of physical change. Though Russell ranks him below Pythagoras, Heraclitus, and Parmenides in stature, he treats him as historically important both as a transitional figure carrying Ionian rationalism into Athens and as an influence on Socrates.
historical_background: Anaxagoras was born around 500 B.C. at Clazomenae in Ionia and spent roughly thirty years (c. 462-432 B.C.) in Athens, likely brought there by Pericles, who wanted to civilize his fellow citizens; Russell speculates Aspasia (also from Ionia) may have introduced them. As Pericles aged, political opponents attacked him indirectly by prosecuting his associates: Pheidias was accused of embezzling gold meant for his statues, and a new law permitting impeachment of those who failed to practise religion or who taught theories about 'the things on high' was used to prosecute Anaxagoras for teaching that the sun was a red-hot stone and the moon was earth. He was forced to leave Athens, apparently rescued by Pericles, and returned to Ionia, where he founded a school; the anniversary of his death was kept afterward as a schoolchildren's holiday.
philosophical_problems: What explains motion and change in the physical world: mechanical necessity or a directing mind?
How can matter be infinitely divisible while things still have distinct, recognizable qualities?
Is there a fundamental difference between living/intelligent things and inert matter, and what accounts for it?
Does introducing 'mind' as a cosmic cause actually do explanatory work, or is it invoked only when other explanations run out?

philosophers_discussed.name: Anaxagoras
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: The chapter's subject: an Ionian rationalist who introduced philosophy to Athens, proposed 'mind' (nous) as the cause of cosmic motion and of the difference between living and dead matter, held that everything contains a portion of everything (except mind), and made genuine scientific contributions (correct theory of eclipses, moon shining by reflected light).

philosophers_discussed.name: Pericles
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Brought Anaxagoras to Athens and later helped him escape prosecution and leave the city.

philosophers_discussed.name: Empedocles
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Compared to Anaxagoras: both argue against the existence of a void, citing devices like the clepsydra (water-clock) or an inflated skin to show that apparently empty space contains air.

philosophers_discussed.name: Aristotle
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Cited as criticizing Anaxagoras for introducing mind as a cosmic cause but then making little use of it, resorting to mechanical explanation whenever possible.

philosophers_discussed.name: Socrates
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Russell notes that the Platonic Socrates joins Aristotle in complaining that Anaxagoras underuses the concept of mind once he has introduced it; Anaxagoras is also named as an influence helping to form Socrates.

core_concepts.name: Nous (Mind) as cosmic cause
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Anaxagoras said that a special, pure substance called 'Mind' set the universe spinning and is what makes living things different from dead matter, unlike everything else, which is mixed with everything else.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Anaxagoras's doctrine that mind (nous) is a substance distinct from and unmixed with all other matter, infinite and self-ruled, which enters into living things and is the source of all motion, originating a rotation that gradually spreads through the world, sending light things to the circumference and heavy things toward the center.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It marks the first attempt in the tradition Russell surveys to give a non-mechanical, quasi-teleological cause (mind) alongside or instead of purely material explanation, and it is a direct forerunner of Socrates's interest (via Anaxagoras) in mind as an explanatory principle, later developed very differently by Plato and Aristotle.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed by Anaxagoras in Ionia and during his years in Athens (c. 462-432 B.C.).
examples: Mind causing the original rotation that separates light and heavy matter
Mind as the differentiating factor between living and dead matter
objections: Aristotle and the Platonic Socrates both complain that Anaxagoras, having introduced mind, makes very little use of it, resorting to mechanical explanation whenever he can.
Aristotle points out Anaxagoras invokes mind as a cause only when he has no other explanation available.
competing_positions: The Atomists' fully mechanical account of motion and vortex-formation, explicitly contrasted by Russell as an advance over explaining vortices by 'the action of mind'
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Socrates professed to have learned from Anaxagoras the idea of the pre-eminence of mind in creation, though he was later disappointed (per the Phaedo, referenced by Russell's broader discussion) that Anaxagoras did not use mind to explain things teleologically.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Anaxagoras's naturalistic claims (sun as a red-hot stone, moon as earth) were the basis of his prosecution for impiety under a law targeting those who taught theories about 'the things on high.'

core_concepts.name: Universal mixture / infinite divisibility of matter
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Anaxagoras thought every piece of matter, no matter how small, contains a bit of every kind of stuff there is; something just looks like 'fire' or 'water' because that ingredient predominates in it.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that matter is infinitely divisible and that every portion of matter, however small, contains some portion of every element; a thing is called by the name of whichever element preponderates within it (e.g., something is called 'fire' because fire predominates, though it also contains portions of everything else, including, Anaxagoras held, some blackness even in snow).
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is Anaxagoras's distinctive solution to the problem, shared with other post-Parmenidean philosophers, of accounting for apparent change and plurality without admitting real coming-into-being or passing-away of substance.
core_concepts.historical_origin: A response to Parmenides's arguments against absolute generation and destruction, worked out independently of Empedocles's four-element theory.
examples: Everything contains some fire, but is only called 'fire' if fire predominates
Snow is (in part) black, according to Anaxagoras
competing_positions: Empedocles's theory of four unchanging elements (earth, air, fire, water) mixed in different proportions

core_concepts.name: Argument against the void
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Anaxagoras argued there is no truly empty space; apparently empty containers, like an inflated skin or a water-clock, actually contain air.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Like Empedocles, Anaxagoras denied the existence of a void, appealing to the observation that devices such as the clepsydra (water-clock) or an inflated skin demonstrate the presence of air where nothing visible seems to be present.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: This is part of the broader fifth-century debate (continued in the next chapter on the Atomists) over whether motion requires empty space, and it shows the era's characteristic mixture of empirical observation and metaphysical argument.
competing_positions: The Atomists' insistence, discussed in the following chapter, that a void must exist for motion to be possible

core_concepts.name: Mind as uniform across living things
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Anaxagoras thought mind is the same in quality in every living thing, including animals; humans only seem smarter because they have hands, not because their minds are inherently superior.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The claim that nous is uniform and equally present ('just as good') in animals as in man, with apparent differences of intelligence between species attributed entirely to bodily differences, especially the possession of hands.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: An unusually egalitarian and materialist twist on the mind-doctrine, since it denies any qualitative superiority of human reason over animal reason.
examples: Man's apparent superiority attributed to having hands, not superior mind

arguments.title: Argument against the void from the clepsydra/inflated skin
premises: A water-clock (clepsydra) or an inflated skin appears, to ordinary observation, to enclose empty space.
Careful use of these devices shows that resistance and displacement occur exactly as if air were present in the apparently empty space.
arguments.conclusion: There is no true void; what seems to be empty space is in fact filled with air.
arguments.explanation: This is an empirical argument, appealing to a physical demonstration rather than pure logic, and Russell classes it alongside Empedocles's identical use of the same evidence. It reflects the era's blending of observation and metaphysical argument, later contrasted with the Atomists, who accepted the reality of a void despite similar evidence.
implications: Denies the Atomists' central postulate of empty space, setting up the dispute treated fully in the next chapter.

arguments.title: Aristotle's criticism that Anaxagoras underuses mind as an explanatory cause
premises: Anaxagoras introduces mind (nous) as the source of cosmic motion and of the distinction between living and dead matter.
In practice, whenever a mechanical explanation is available, Anaxagoras gives that instead.
Anaxagoras invokes mind as a cause only in cases where he knows no other cause.
arguments.conclusion: Anaxagoras's introduction of mind does little real explanatory work in his system as a whole.
arguments.explanation: Russell reports this as a joint complaint of Aristotle and the Platonic Socrates: having made the innovative move of positing mind as a cosmic cause, Anaxagoras largely reverts to mechanical explanation, so the doctrine functions more as a stopgap for otherwise unexplained phenomena (like the initial rotation) than as a thoroughgoing teleological principle.
implications: Anticipates Socrates's disappointment (elsewhere in Plato) that Anaxagoras did not use mind to show that everything is for the best.
Marks a contrast with the fully mechanistic Atomists discussed next, whom Russell treats as more consistent.

key_distinctions: Mechanical/material causation versus mind (nous) as a directing cause
Elements that are 'in' a thing versus the element that predominates and gives the thing its name
Mind as unmixed and pure versus ordinary matter, which contains a portion of everything
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell notes all Anaxagoras's predecessors influenced him except Pythagoras, and that Parmenides influenced him as he had influenced Empedocles (motivating the denial of real generation/destruction and the postulate that matter must be conserved). He is said to belong to the school of Anaximenes and continues the Ionian rationalist and scientific tradition.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Anaxagoras is presented as the crucial link who first brought philosophy to Athens and helped form Socrates, who took from him the idea of mind's pre-eminence in creation, even though (as Russell notes) Anaxagoras lacked the ethical and religious preoccupations that later passed from the Pythagoreans through Socrates to Plato.
political_social_context: Prosecuted under an Athenian law permitting impeachment of those who failed to practise religion and taught theories about 'the things on high'; this followed a political campaign by opponents of the aging Pericles, who attacked his associates (Pheidias, then Anaxagoras) as an indirect way of weakening him. The same charge of impiety concerning the sun and moon was later revived against Socrates.
religion_science_culture_context: Anaxagoras gave the correct scientific account that the moon shines by reflected light and the correct theory of eclipses; he held the sun and stars are fiery stones (the sun larger than the Peloponnese), that we do not feel starlight's heat because of distance, and that the moon has mountains and, he thought, inhabitants. Russell judges he probably was not concerned with ethics or religion and was probably an atheist, as his prosecutors alleged.
russell_presentation: Russell presents Anaxagoras as a figure of real but secondary historical importance: not the equal of Pythagoras, Heraclitus, or Parmenides, but significant as the Ionian who first brought philosophy to Athens and first proposed mind as the primary cause of physical change. Russell narrates his biography (birth at Clazomenae, decades in Athens under Pericles's patronage, prosecution for impiety, exile back to Ionia) and his doctrines: infinite divisibility of matter with each portion containing something of every element except mind; denial of the void via the clepsydra argument; and mind as a pure, unmixed substance that both distinguishes living things from dead matter and causes the cosmic rotation separating light from heavy matter. Russell reports, without fully endorsing, Aristotle's and the Platonic Socrates's shared complaint that Anaxagoras underuses his own concept of mind, preferring mechanical explanations wherever available and invoking mind only as a last resort. Russell credits him with genuine scientific merit, above all the correct explanations of moonlight and eclipses, and closes by noting that, unlike his philosophical successors from the Pythagoreans through Socrates to Plato, Anaxagoras lacked their ethical and religious preoccupations, which Russell elsewhere treats as having introduced an 'obscurantist bias' into Greek philosophy.
critical_context: Interpretive point flagged by Russell himself: there is scholarly uncertainty about exactly what happened at Anaxagoras's trial (he says 'what happened is not certain, except that he had to leave Athens'), and about the degree of direct influence Anaxagoras had on Euripides, which Russell calls 'more doubtful.' These are presented by Russell as open historical questions rather than settled fact.
key_takeaways: Anaxagoras was the first philosopher to bring philosophy to Athens and the first to propose mind (nous) as the primary cause of physical change.
He held that matter is infinitely divisible and that everything contains a portion of every element except mind; a thing is named for whichever element predominates in it.
Mind, for Anaxagoras, is pure and unmixed with everything else, and is the source of the cosmic rotation that sorts light matter to the edge and heavy matter to the center.
He was prosecuted for impiety (teaching the sun was a red-hot stone and the moon was earth) as an indirect political attack on his patron Pericles, and had to leave Athens.
Both Aristotle and the Platonic Socrates criticized him for introducing mind as a cause but then relying on mechanical explanation wherever possible.
He made genuine scientific contributions: the correct theory that moonlight is reflected sunlight and the correct explanation of eclipses.
study_notes:
Anaxagoras occupies an important hinge position in Russell's narrative. Geographically and intellectually he belongs to the Ionian rationalist tradition of Anaximenes and Anaximander; biographically, he is the person who physically relocates that tradition to Athens, decades before Socrates or Plato make Athens the philosophical capital of Greece in their own right. Keep the two halves of his doctrine distinct when studying him. First, there is his theory of matter: infinite divisibility, with every portion of stuff containing a share of every element, so that what we call 'fire' or 'water' is really just a mixture in which one ingredient predominates. This is his answer to the Parmenidean puzzle about how change and plurality are possible without true coming-to-be or passing-away, and it runs in parallel to, but independently of, Empedocles's four-element theory covered elsewhere in Russell's account.

Second, and more historically influential, there is his theory of mind (nous) as a substance categorically different from ordinary matter: unmixed, infinite, self-ruled, and the source of all motion and of the distinction between living and dead things. This is philosophically significant less for what Anaxagoras actually did with it (Russell reports that he mostly did not use it, falling back on mechanical explanation) than for what it suggested to others: Socrates, according to Plato, initially hoped Anaxagoras's 'mind' would explain the world teleologically, i.e., show that everything happens for the best, and was disappointed to find Anaxagoras using mind merely as a mechanical trigger for a cosmic rotation. This disappointment matters for understanding why Socrates and Plato later develop their own, very different, teleological accounts of mind and value. When you reach the next chapter on the Atomists, notice the explicit contrast Russell draws: the Atomists explain the same kind of vortex-formation Anaxagoras attributes to mind through purely mechanical collision, which Russell calls 'an advance.'

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Anaxagoras's name for a special, pure kind of 'stuff' that causes motion and makes living things different from non-living matter.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: In Anaxagoras's system, a substance distinct from and unmixed with all other matter, infinite and self-ruled, that enters into the composition of living things and originates the cosmic rotation that produces motion and the separation of light and heavy matter.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that every tiny bit of matter contains a little of everything, not just one pure substance.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Anaxagoras's doctrine that matter is infinitely divisible and every portion, however small, contains some share of every element except mind; things are named for the element that predominates in them.
related_concepts: Universal mixture / infinite divisibility of matter

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: An Athenian law that made it a crime not to practice the state religion or to teach unconventional theories about the heavens.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A law permitting the impeachment of those who did not practise religion or who taught theories about 'the things on high,' used to prosecute Anaxagoras for his naturalistic claims about the sun and moon, and later revived against Socrates.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The correct scientific idea that the moon does not produce its own light but shines because it reflects sunlight.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: A doctrine Russell credits Anaxagoras with first clearly explaining, alongside the correct theory of eclipses and the knowledge that the moon lies below the sun.

questions.prompt: What two 'firsts' does Russell credit to Anaxagoras?
questions.answer: He was the first to introduce philosophy to the Athenians, and the first to suggest mind as the primary cause of physical changes.
questions.explanation: These are the two claims Russell opens the chapter with to establish Anaxagoras's historical importance despite ranking him below Pythagoras, Heraclitus, and Parmenides.

questions.prompt: Which Athenian statesman is thought to have brought Anaxagoras to Athens, and why was he later prosecuted?
questions.answer: Pericles brought him to Athens; Anaxagoras was later prosecuted under a law against impiety for teaching that the sun was a red-hot stone and the moon was earth, as part of a political campaign against Pericles's associates.
questions.explanation: The prosecution targeted Pericles indirectly by attacking his friends, first Pheidias, then Anaxagoras.

questions.prompt: Explain Anaxagoras's doctrine of universal mixture: why is something called 'fire' rather than something else?
questions.answer: Because every portion of matter, however small, contains some of every element; a thing is called by the name of whichever element preponderates in it, so something is called 'fire' because fire is the predominant ingredient, even though it also contains traces of everything else.
questions.explanation: This is Anaxagoras's account of how apparently distinct kinds of matter can exist given his commitment to infinite divisibility and universal mixture.

questions.prompt: Compare Anaxagoras's mind-caused vortex with the Atomists' account of vortex-formation, as Russell frames the contrast.
questions.answer: Anaxagoras attributes the cosmic rotation that sorts light and heavy matter to the action of mind (nous); the Atomists, discussed in the following chapter, explain a similar vortex mechanically, through the collisions of atoms, which Russell calls 'an advance' over explaining it by the action of mind.
questions.explanation: Russell explicitly draws this contrast when introducing the Atomists' cosmology.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct Aristotle's and the Platonic Socrates's shared criticism of Anaxagoras's use of the concept of mind.
questions.answer: Anaxagoras introduces mind as the cause of cosmic motion and as what distinguishes living from dead matter; however, in practice he gives mechanical explanations wherever he can, and introduces mind as a cause only when he knows of no other. The criticism concludes that, having made this innovative move, Anaxagoras does little with it.
questions.explanation: This argument-reconstruction question tests whether the student can lay out the premises and conclusion of the criticism Russell reports.

questions.prompt: What two genuine scientific achievements does Russell credit to Anaxagoras?
questions.answer: He first clearly explained that the moon shines by reflected light, and he gave the correct theory of eclipses, also knowing that the moon is below the sun.
questions.explanation: Russell notes these achievements despite his generally modest overall assessment of Anaxagoras's philosophical rank.

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, what was Anaxagoras the first philosopher to do?
quiz.explanation: Russell credits Anaxagoras as the first to bring philosophy to Athens and the first to propose mind as the primary cause of physical change.

quiz.prompt: What was Anaxagoras formally accused of that led to his prosecution?
options: Teaching that the sun was a red-hot stone and the moon was earth
quiz.explanation: He was prosecuted under an impiety law for these naturalistic astronomical claims; the same charge was later revived against Socrates.

quiz.prompt: In Anaxagoras's doctrine of universal mixture, why is a thing called 'fire' rather than something else?
options: Because it contains only fire and nothing else
Because fire is the element that predominates in it, though it contains portions of all elements
Because Anaxagoras arbitrarily assigned the name
quiz.explanation: Every portion of matter contains some of every element except mind; a thing is called by whichever element preponderates.
quiz.related_concept: Universal mixture / infinite divisibility of matter

quiz.prompt: According to Russell, both Aristotle and the Platonic Socrates praised Anaxagoras for consistently using mind to explain events throughout his system.
quiz.explanation: False: both criticized him for introducing mind but then relying mainly on mechanical explanations, invoking mind only when no other cause was available.

quiz.prompt: What evidence did Anaxagoras (like Empedocles) use to argue against the existence of a void?
options: The clepsydra (water-clock) and an inflated skin showing air is present
quiz.explanation: Both philosophers appealed to these devices to show that apparently empty space actually contains air.

quiz.prompt: Anaxagoras held that mind is uniform across living things, and that man's apparent intellectual superiority over animals is really due to his possession of ______.
quiz.explanation: Russell reports that Anaxagoras attributed apparent differences in intelligence to bodily differences, especially the possession of hands, since mind itself is equally good in animals as in man.
quiz.related_concept: Mind as uniform across living things

quiz.prompt: Which correct astronomical fact does Russell credit to Anaxagoras?
options: That the earth orbits the sun
That the moon shines by reflected light
That the stars are other suns with planets
That the sun is a god
quiz.explanation: Anaxagoras is credited with first clearly explaining that moonlight is reflected sunlight, and with the correct theory of eclipses.

(1) prosecuted him; (2) was his teacher; (3) exiled him; (4) refuted his physics
(1) wrote his biography; (2) was his rival in Ionia; (3) never mentioned him; (4) denied he existed
